fig13_1: Two side-by-side panels for the inhomogeneous Poisson problem solved by the lifting technique. The left panel plots the solution u against x on the interval minus one to one, with open circles for the spectral result lying on top of a solid reference curve for N equal to sixteen, the solution rising from zero at the left to one at the right. The right panel is a semilog plot of maximum error against N, the points falling along a straight line that descends to about machine precision, ten to the power minus sixteen, near N equal to twenty, confirming geometric spectral convergence.
fig13_2: Two panels for the Helmholtz equation with a Robin left boundary at wavenumber k equal to two and N equal to thirty-two. The left panel plots solution u against x for four values of the Robin parameter alpha equal to zero (Neumann), one, five, and twenty; as alpha increases the curves are progressively pulled down toward zero at the left endpoint x equal to minus one, showing the smooth transition from Neumann toward Dirichlet behaviour. The right panel is a semilog plot of maximum error versus N for alpha equal to five, the points dropping in a straight line to near machine precision, the signature of spectral convergence.
fig13_3: Semilog plot of the condition number of the discrete Robin Helmholtz operator against the Robin parameter alpha, with three curves for N equal to sixteen, thirty-two, and sixty-four. Each curve stays at a moderate level across the full range of alpha, with the larger N giving uniformly larger condition numbers, illustrating that conditioning grows only polynomially with N and depends only mildly on alpha, so the tau row-replacement approach remains numerically robust.
fig13_4: Space-time color map of the Allen-Cahn solution with fixed Dirichlet boundaries at minus one and plus one and small parameter epsilon equal to zero point zero one, with horizontal axis position x and vertical axis time. Three nearly vertical transition layers separating the plus and minus phases appear at the start and persist almost unchanged for a long interval, the metastable regime, until near time forty-five two of the interfaces abruptly merge and annihilate, leaving a single central interface fixed by the boundary data.
fig13_5: Space-time color map of the Allen-Cahn solution with an oscillating right boundary equal to one plus sine squared of t over five, horizontal axis position x and vertical axis time. Compared with the fixed-boundary case, the driven boundary pumps energy in, shifting the surviving equilibrium interface leftward to about x equal to minus zero point four and triggering the annihilation of the extra interfaces earlier, near time thirty.
fig13_6: Two panels for the radiative cooling problem with N equal to thirty-two. The left panel plots temperature profiles u against x at times zero, zero point one, zero point five, one, and five for radiation strength sigma equal to one; the curves start flat at one and progressively drop near the right boundary as heat radiates away, approaching a steady state. The right panel plots the right-boundary temperature u at x equal to one versus time for sigma equal to zero point one, one, and ten, showing that larger sigma produces faster and deeper cooling of the surface.
fig13_7: Three-dimensional surface plot of the harmonic solution of the Laplace equation on the square minus one to one in both x and y, computed with N equal to twenty-four. The smooth surface is flat (zero) over most of the boundary but rises into a hump driven by the sine-to-the-fourth-power of pi x data along the upper-left edge and undulates along the right edge following the sine of three pi y over five oscillation, with the interior smoothly interpolating between these to satisfy Laplace's equation to spectral accuracy.
fig13_8: Scatter plot of computed quasinormal-mode eigenvalues in the complex frequency plane for the Poeschl-Teller potential with barrier height V-zero equal to two, N equal to eighty, and truncation length L equal to eight; the horizontal axis is the real part of omega and the vertical axis the imaginary part. Many grey dots are scattered across the plane, these being spurious artefacts of domain truncation and companion linearisation. A star marks the computed fundamental mode near plus or minus one point three two three minus zero point five i, overlapping a cross at the exact Ferrari-Mashhoon value, the two agreeing to about four significant digits.
fig13_9: Two panels showing the eigenfunctions of the first two quasinormal modes plotted against position x. The left panel shows the fundamental mode, index n equal to zero, with a single antinode (one main peak) centred on the potential peak at the origin. The right panel shows the first overtone, index n equal to one, with one nodal crossing through zero. In both panels the tails at large absolute x oscillate and grow, reflecting the outgoing and ingoing wave boundary conditions characteristic of quasinormal modes.
fig13_10: Two semilog convergence panels for the fundamental quasinormal frequency omega-zero. The left panel plots the error against the number of points N at fixed truncation length L equal to eight: the error first falls steeply (spectral convergence) but then flattens onto a plateau near two times ten to the power minus four set by domain truncation. The right panel plots the error against truncation length L at fixed N equal to eighty: the error decays exponentially up to about L equal to nine, then turns and rises again as the fixed grid becomes too coarse to resolve the wider domain, revealing an optimal L.
fig13_11: Two panels for the vibrating string fixed at one end and free at the other, computed with N equal to thirty-six. The left panel overlays the first six numerical eigenmodes as solid curves on the exact quarter-wavelength sine eigenfunctions as dashed curves over x in zero to one, the two sets coinciding; successive modes add half-wavelengths. The right panel is a semilog plot of eigenvalue error versus mode number, the error tiny for low modes then rising sharply, showing that roughly the first two-thirds of N eigenvalues are resolved accurately before the grid resolution limit.
